paragraphs.heading: A number that depends on chance
paragraphs.text: A random variable is a rule that takes each possible outcome of a chance situation and gives back a value. The set of all possible outcomes is called the sample space, often written Ω. Usually the values are real numbers, and random variables are usually named with capital letters such as X, Y, Z or T. One particular value that actually turns up is called a random variate. According to George Mackey, Pafnuty Chebyshev was the first to think systematically in terms of random variables.

paragraphs.heading: What the randomness stands for
paragraphs.text: The chance behind a random variable can be something like the roll of a die. It can also stand for uncertainty, such as an error in a measurement. What probability really means is a hard philosophical question. The mathematics, though, does not depend on settling it, and can rest on a strict set of axioms instead.

paragraphs.heading: Discrete or continuous
paragraphs.text: When a random variable can take only a finite list of values, or an endless list that can still be counted off, it is called discrete. Its pattern of chances can be given by a probability mass function, which assigns a probability to each value. When the possible values are uncountably many, usually a whole interval, the variable is called continuous. In the absolutely continuous case a probability density function describes it by giving probabilities to intervals, and every single point then has probability zero.

paragraphs.heading: From variable to distribution
paragraphs.text: For a real-valued X you can ask questions like how likely it is that X equals 2. Writing down all such probabilities gives the probability distribution of X. The distribution keeps only how likely each output is and forgets the particular sample space that X was built on. For a real-valued X it can always be summed up by the cumulative distribution function, F_X(x) = P (X ≤ x), the chance that X is at most x.

paragraphs.heading: Same distribution, different variables
paragraphs.text: Two random variables can share exactly the same distribution and still differ in important ways. For example, they may be independent of each other. The sample space is what makes it possible to define ideas like correlation and independence, through the joint distribution of several variables on the same space. In practice people often drop the sample space entirely and just work with probability distributions.

paragraphs.heading: Values beyond ordinary numbers
paragraphs.text: The same definition works for values of many other kinds, not only real numbers. There can be random Boolean values, categories, complex numbers, vectors, matrices, trees, shapes and even functions; these more general versions are sometimes called random elements. A random word, for instance, can be treated as a random whole number that points to an entry in a vocabulary list. A random graph on N given vertices can be held as an N × N grid of random variables that together describe the graph.
